sections.html: The South American pufferfish Colomesus asellus (a recent study shows that, based on genetic analysis, the genus Colomesus should be considered a synonym of Sphoeroides; the species should therefore correctly be designated as Sphoeroides asellus) is ideal for aquarium keeping. It remains small (usually around 6–8 cm, at most around 12 cm; other size claims are based on misidentification), is a strictly freshwater species, loves to eat small snails, and is completely peaceful, both toward conspecifics and other fish species.

The Amazon puffer, Colomesus asellus, is a freshwater puffer found throughout much of the Amazon basin, with records north to Guyana and Venezuela. Also traded as the South American puffer or 'SAP', it is told from congeners by a transverse row of dermal flaps across the chin. It lives mostly in well-oxygenated river habitats, is intolerant of organic waste, and forms loose aggregations, so a group of 6 or more is best, away from the general community.
The fish are sourced from the upper Amazon, mostly from Peru, but sometimes also from Colombia or Brazil.

Occurs throughout much of the Amazon basin in Brazil, Colombia, Peru, and Ecuador, including the Amazonas/Solimões main channel plus the rios Pará, Tocantins, Jari, Xingu, Tapajós, Uatumã, Madeira, Trombetas, Negro, Purus, Tefé, Japurá/Caquetá, Juruá, Jutaí, Içá/Putomayo, Javary, Ampiyacu, Amacayacú, Napo, Nanay, Marañón, and Ucayali, with its range extending at least as far upstream as Pucallpa in eastern Peru.

There are also numerous records from drainages north of the Amazon mouth including the Essequibo and Waini in Guyana, and lower Orinoco in Venezuela. It appears to be absent from French Guiana and Suriname.

Type locality is 'Barama River, northwestern Guyana'.

Has been recorded in lower, middle, and upper river basins with habitats including sandbars, beaches, floodplain lakes, banks with overhanging vegetation, and fast-flowing rapids over bedrock, boulders, and stones. It is mostly collected from habitats with high oxygen levels, suggesting that it may be sensitive to low oxygen availability.

It is adaptable, penetrating into tributaries of the upper Amazon, but also occuring in the Amazon and Orinoco delta regions, although it does not tend to be found in highly acidic black-waters.
An aquarium with base dimensions of 120 × 30 × 30 cm or larger is required for long-term care (about 108 litres).

Special care is needed during the acclimation period: Colomesus are highly susceptible to Piscinoodinum and Ichthyophthirius (velvet and white spot disease). These diseases can be effectively treated with commercially available medications; additionally, raising the temperature to 30°C and using a flow pump can help. Once acclimated, however, the fish are hardy and long-lived, and their playful nature brings a lot of joy.

Choice of décor is not especially critical though it should be maintained in a well-decorated set-up. The addition of floating or overhanging vegetation and driftwood roots or branches also seems to be appreciated.

This species is intolerant of organic waste and require spotless water in order to thrive. Moderate levels of dissolved oxygen and water movement are also recommended, meaning additional powerheads, pumps, etc., should be employed as necessary. A linear flow pump may prove a useful addition, while weekly water changes of 30-50% should be considered mandatory.

Wild examples can be delicate and sensitive to white spot/ich post-import, so a lengthy quarantine period may be required.

• Temperature: 20–26°C
  • pH: 5.5–8.0
  • Hardness: 2–15 dGH

Tetraodontids lack true teeth, the jawbone itself being modified into four fused toothlike structures. These grow continuously at a surprising rate, so offer regular meals of shelled invertebrates such as snails, crab legs, cockles, etc., in order to maintain them at a reasonable length. There is some evidence to suggest that aufwuchs form a significant proportion of the natural diet, therefore it may be worth permitting or even encouraging algal growth on hard items of décor.

Additional foods can include chopped shellfish, small earthworms, and live or frozen chironomid larvae (bloodworm), Artemia, etc. Dried products should not form the principal component of the diet, although pelleted formats with a very hard consistency may prove useful.

They have only one trait that counts against them: they are incredibly active and dart around the aquarium nonstop. Under no circumstances should they be kept with fish species that prefer quiet, and even nervous aquarists should steer clear of them.

Not aggressive as such but unsuitable for the general community aquarium, and best-maintained alone or in a larger set-up with other fluvial fishes.

This species naturally forms loose aggregations and can behave nervously in the absence of conspecifics. Ideally a group of 6 or more should be purchased.
Unconfirmed.

Unrecorded in aquaria.

This species exhibits a spawning strategy comparable to that of marine puffers and in contrast to the majority of freshwater tetraodontids, with high fecundity, relatively small eggs, and no parental care. Limited studies in the central Amazon basin suggest that spawning occurs in main river channels or close to banks at the mouths of floodplain lakes and tributaries during periods of high water. The pelagic larvae are washed into nursery zones in floodplain lakes where they complete their development, returning to river channels when flood waters recede.

A look-alike species was described in 2013 from the Rio Tocantins basin in Brazil; it is virtually indistinguishable from S. asellus in color, but differs in minor anatomical details and, most notably, based on DNA: Sphoeroides tocantinensis. This species is also a strictly freshwater pufferfish. To the best of our knowledge, it is not exported, and its care should not differ from that of S. asellus.

This species is also referred to as 'South American puffer', 'SAP', 'Amazonian puffer', 'Peruvian puffer', or 'Brazilian puffer' in the ornamental trade.

Within the genus Colomesus, C. asellus can be immediately identified by possessing a unique transverse row of dermal flaps across the chin which is absent in its congeners C. psittacus and C. tocantinensis. It can be further told apart from the very similar C. tocantinensis by possession of 10 (vs. 9 in C. tocantinensis) anal-fin rays, 11 (vs. 10) dorsal-fin rays, a triangular (vs. notched ventrally, appearing as an inverted V) opercle, base colour in dorsal portion of body golden yellow (vs. light yellow to pale).

It is distinguished from C. psittacus by its smaller adult size (max. 128 mm SL vs. 289 mm in SL in C. psittacus), possession of 13-16 (vs. 17-19) pectoral-fin rays, presence of 5 (vs. 6) transverse dark bands dorsally on the body, and predominantly freshwater, fluvial (vs. brackish, coastal) ecology.

Tetraodontids are commonly referred to as 'puffers' due to the ability of many species to inflate their body to an enormous size when stressed or threatened. This is achieved by drawing water into a specialised ventral diverticulum of the stomach, although air can also be used if the fish is removed from the water. As a result of these morphological adaptations puffers swim via a unique combination of pectoral and median fin undulations referred to as 'diodontiform' swimming. They are also able to produce sounds by grinding the jaw/pharyngeal teeth or vibrating the swim bladder. Puffers are secondary freshwater fishes, with the majority of members exclusively inhabiting marine environments.

Other defining characters of tetraodontids include a tough skin usually covered with small spines, a beak-like dental plate divided by a median suture, a reduced gill opening anterior to the pectoral-fin base, no pelvic fins or spinous fin rays, typically short-based dorsal and anal fins, and no ribs.

Puffer flesh is toxic and can cause clinical poisoning and human mortality, although it is regarded as a delicacy in certain countries. The predominant toxin, usually either tetrodotoxin or saxitoxin, is dependant on species, geographic area, and time of year. The toxins are not produced by the fishes themselves, but by bacteria living in symbiotic association, or they are acquired via the food chain. Colomesus species accumulate saxitoxin, although it is unclear whether eating their flesh represents a danger to humans.

Colomesus asellus is known as the Amazon puffer and South American puffer (SAP). It grows to about 7.6 cm and is one of the few freshwater "community puffers". Its golden yellow body is covered with splotchy, dark bands like a bumblebee pattern, with a white underbelly and a black spot near the base of the tail. Hobbyists have reported keeping them for 8-10 years and sometimes longer.

Fish farms have not yet found a way to breed Amazon puffers profitably in captivity, so all those sold in stores are wild-caught. Many arrive extremely skinny with parasitic infections. Do not buy a puffer that has a concave abdomen or is covered in white spots. Even healthy-looking specimens should be quarantined in a separate tank first so they do not spread diseases to other aquariums.

Because of the high likelihood of pathogens, it is recommended to proactively treat them with a trio of quarantine medications to clear any bacterial, fungal or parasitic illnesses.

How do you deworm a puffer? Pufferfish are especially prone to internal parasites such as tapeworms, but dewormers only remove adult worms and do not affect unhatched eggs, so multiple treatments are needed. One approach: treat with the quarantine medication trio and wait two weeks. Next, give a 5-day treatment of Fritz ParaCleanse (following the instructions on the box) and wait a month. Finally, use a 7-day treatment of PraziPro as the last deworming step.
The Amazon puffer is found throughout the Amazon basin and surrounding areas.
It lives in many different habitats, from floodplain lakes to rushing rivers.

Because these puffers are fairly active swimmers, keep them in at least a 114-litre aquarium; 208 litres would be even better. Add lots of decorations, plants and hardscape to block lines of sight and give them areas to explore. Tall background plants such as vallisneria act as moving obstacles to swim around, providing enrichment.
Because they live in such a wide variety of habitats, they are quite hardy and can be kept at pH 6.0-8.0, in soft or hard water, at 22-28°C.

Like many puffers, SAPs have four continually growing teeth at the front of the mouth forming a "beak", which lets them crush the hard shells of crustaceans and mollusks. To stop the teeth from becoming too long, feed all sorts of crunchy foods such as bladder snails, ramshorn snails and freeze-dried krill. Some hobbyists have successfully fed Repashy gel food mixed with crushed oyster shells (sold as chicken feed), or dipped rocks in Repashy so the puffers scrape their teeth on hard surfaces.

If newly purchased puffers struggle to gain weight, try frozen bloodworms and live blackworms at first. These do not help file the teeth down, but few puffers can resist them. Then transition to hard, crunchy foods.

How do you clip a pufferfish's teeth? If hard foods do not wear the beak down enough, the teeth may become so overgrown that the fish can no longer eat properly. To prevent starvation, clip the tips of the teeth with sharp cuticle trimmers. A common technique is to add 2-4 drops of clove oil per 1 litre of water. Place the puffer in this mild anesthetic solution and it should be sedated within a minute or two. Hold the drowsy puffer gently in your fist; if it is too slippery, use surgical gloves or a fish net wrapped around it like a blanket. Trim off the pointy tips of the upper and lower teeth as needed. Return the fish to fresh water and it should wake within a few minutes. Depending on the puffer and its diet, this may need repeating every 4-12 months.

South American puffers are very curious and like to closely examine every nook and cranny. They can suck in water or air to puff up as a defense mechanism, but do not deliberately stress them to see this. When transporting them, use a small plastic tub or catch cup instead of a net to prevent them from sucking in air.

They are best kept either individually or in a group of six or more; a number in between may lead to fighting and territorial disputes.

Tankmates: They are considered "community fish" compared to other puffers, but still have attitude and can nip slower, long-finned fish. They also tend to eat invertebrates such as snails and shrimp. Keep them with similar-sized, peaceful, energetic fish such as mollies, swordtails, larger tetras and rasboras, and dwarf cichlids.

Glass surfing: Repeatedly swimming up and down the tank walls may be caused by stress, boredom, territory defense and other reasons. There is no guaranteed cure, but hobbyists have tried covering or painting the tank walls black to reduce reflection, increasing flow with a powerhead, blocking a favorite corner with tall decorations or plants, adding tannins with catappa leaves to reduce visibility, and feeding different live foods to hunt.
